sections.title: Name and classification
sections.text: Index Fungorum uses Collybia sordida (Schumach.) Z.M. He & Zhu L. Yang, a combination published in 2023 in a phylogenetic revision of Clitocybaceae. However, GBIF/Catalogue of Life still accepts Lepista sordida and treats Collybia sordida as a synonym; many field guides also retain the older name. Generic placement is therefore not harmonized. Index Fungorum places the species in Agaricales and Clitocybaceae.

sections.title: Appearance
sections.text: A small gilled mushroom, usually more slender than the wood blewit Collybia nuda. The cap starts convex and later flattens or becomes slightly depressed at the centre; its smooth surface is hygrophanous: lilac or greyish violet when moist, it fades on drying towards pinkish beige, sometimes with a more olive-toned centre. The fairly crowded gills are lilac at first and later pale; they are adnate to slightly decurrent. The thin, fibrillose and often sinuous stem is lilac to greyish or whitish, with white mycelium at the base; it has no ring or volva.

sections.title: Habitat and ecology
sections.text: This is a saprotrophic fungus growing on organic-rich soil among grass and litter, including lawns, gardens, parks and woodland edges. It can fruit in small groups or fairy rings. Documented collections from lawns and grassland support that it is not tied to a particular tree species.

sections.title: Lookalikes and caution
sections.text: Collybia sordida may be confused with C. nuda, which is generally more robust and less hygrophanous, and with other lilac mushrooms. Purple-gilled Cortinarius species can be dangerous; colour alone cannot rule them out. DGfM and VAPKO lists include the species under its older name Lepista sordida, but that does not identify a specimen from a picture. Seek a local expert's confirmation before any consumption.

traits: Small lilac to greyish-violet agaric; hygrophanous cap fades when dry, sometimes to pinkish beige
Fairly crowded gills, lilac when young then paler, adnate to slightly decurrent
Thin, fibrillose and sometimes sinuous stem, without ring or volva; white mycelium at the base
Saprotroph on organic-rich soil among grass and litter; may fruit in groups or fairy rings
Current name in Index Fungorum: Collybia sordida; Lepista sordida remains a common synonym in books
safetyNote: DGfM and VAPKO recommendation lists include this species under the name Lepista sordida. Lilac mushrooms can resemble one another and some Cortinarius species are dangerous; this entry and its image cannot provide a safe food identification. Have any collection checked by a local expert.
